taxonomyNote: NatureServe (following Crother 2017) spells the name Mohave; others spell it Mojave.
fieldMarks: Slightly greenish tinge to the body, which gives 'Mojave green'; the western rattlesnake lacks the greenish tinge (NPS Parashant).
Tail bands have thick white bands and narrower black bands; the western diamondback's bands are more uniform in width (NPS Saguaro).
Newborns have a single silent button rather than a full rattle (NPS Parashant).
behavior: At lower elevations mainly nocturnal in summer and commonly active in morning and late afternoon in spring and fall; may be active by day in summer at higher elevations (NatureServe).
Above ground March-November, probably most active late April or May through September (NatureServe).
Eats kangaroo rats, ground squirrels, mice, rabbits and other small mammals; lizards are eaten especially by the young (NatureServe).
Uses rodent burrows to overwinter; hibernates alone or in groups of two or three (NPS Parashant; NPS Saguaro).
habitat: Mostly upland desert and lower mountain slopes: barren desert, grassland, open woodland and scrub with creosotebush, palo verde, mesquite or cacti; usually not in broken rocky terrain or dense vegetation (NatureServe).
In spring it commonly coils under a small tree or shrub in early morning (NatureServe).
range: Southern California, southern Nevada and southwestern Utah south through Arizona, southern New Mexico and western Texas into central Mexico; sea level to about 2,530 m (NatureServe).

lookalikes.name: Western diamond-backed rattlesnake
lookalikes.howToTell: Tail bands are more uniform in width and the body lacks the Mohave's greenish tinge (NPS Saguaro; NPS Parashant).

lookalikes.name: Western rattlesnake
lookalikes.howToTell: Lacks the Mohave's greenish tinge (NPS Parashant).
